cards.explanation: The answer is that he is a leper. Naaman, commander of Aram's army, has everything going for him, and then the verse says he was “…but he was a leper.” That little "but" is carrying the WHOLE building. Rank, respect and victories on one side, leprosy on the other. I bet he'd have handed back a medal or two for clear skin.

The answer is True. The girl says, “If only my master would go to the prophet who is in Samaria, he would cure him of his leprosy.” She's the one taken from Israel, and she's the one who points to help. Small voice, big news.

The answer is Israel. The king of Aram says he'll send Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel. That's the land the young girl was taken from, and it's where she said the prophet was. So the whole trip points back at her words. Send a man with a letter to the right address, and sometimes that's half the miracle.

The answer is True. The letter says, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman, so that you may cure him of his leprosy.” Short, direct, no small talk. It's a letter that gets right to the point. The king of Israel reads it and doesn't take it well.

The answer is a fight. The king of Israel says, “Surely you can see that he is seeking a quarrel with me!” A quarrel is a fight. He reads a letter asking for a cure, and he tears his clothes over it. I think that was a rough moment for him.

The answer is that there is a prophet in Israel. Elisha, the man of God, tells the king, “Please let the man come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel.” The king of Israel tore his clothes, and Elisha just says send him over. I think Elisha is pretty calm about it. No panic, just an invitation.

The answer is False. Elisha sends a messenger instead of coming out. The messenger says, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean.” So the instructions come second-hand. I think a man with a full set of horses and chariots might have expected a handshake.

The answer is that Naaman thought Elisha would call on the LORD and wave a hand over the spot. He says, “I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the spot to cure my leprosy.” He had a whole scene pictured in his head. Then a messenger gave him a river instead. Friends, I've pictured plenty of things that came out different, and mine usually just involve burnt edges.

The answer is that he'd do a great thing, so why not this simple one. His servants say, “My father, if the prophet had told you to do some great thing, would you not have done it?” Then they add, “How much more, then, when he tells you, ‘Wash and be cleansed’?” They're calling him "My father" while telling him he's overthinking it. That's some brave, kind talking.

The answer is that his flesh is like the flesh of a little child. The text says his flesh “…was restored and became like that of a little child, and he was clean.” Nothing left behind, nothing half done. That's what happens when he does what the man of God said. Seven dips, one big change.

The answer is that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. Naaman says, “Now I know for sure that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” This is the same man who left angry at the door of Elisha's house. Now he's back, standing in front of Elisha. Seven dips later, he doesn't just say thanks. He says WHO he now knows is God.

The answer is False. Elisha turns Naaman's gift down. He swears by the LORD that he won't take it, and when Naaman keeps pressing, Elisha still says no (2 Kings 5:16). Friends, plenty of people would have said yes by the second push. Not Elisha.

The answer is as much soil as two mules can carry. Naaman says, “please let me, your servant, be given as much soil as a pair of mules can carry.” He wants soil to take home. Then he says he'll never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD. I think that's a man who plans to take something of Israel home with him.

The answer is the LORD. Naaman says, “For your servant will never again make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to any other god but the LORD.” That's a big change from the man who showed up at the door. He's making a promise about who he'll worship. It comes right after he asks for the soil.

The answer is True. Elisha says, “Go in peace…” That's his whole answer after Naaman asks the LORD to forgive him in this matter. Short and simple, and it comes before Naaman travels off. The text doesn't add anything more to it.

The answer is to run after Naaman and get something from him. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, says, “As surely as the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him.” He uses his master's words and then announces his own plan. I think that should have been the red flag. Elisha said no to the gift, and Gehazi decided to go get it anyway.

The answer is silver and clothing for two young men from the sons of the prophets. Gehazi says, “My master has sent me to say, ‘Look, two young men from the sons of the prophets have just now come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.’…” Elisha never sent him with any such message. That's the story Gehazi tells Naaman. Friends, that's a lot of detail for a made-up errand.
The answer is True. Gehazi asks for a talent of silver. Naaman says, “Please, take two talents.” And he urged Gehazi to accept them. So Gehazi walks away with double what he asked for.

The answer is that Gehazi says he did not go anywhere. He tells Elisha, “Your servant did not go anywhere…” That's his answer to Elisha's question, “Gehazi, where have you been?” After running down a chariot, taking silver and storing it in the house, that's what he came up with. I think Elisha didn't need the explanation.

The answer is Naaman. Elisha says, “Therefore, the leprosy of Naaman will cling to you and your descendants forever!” The same leprosy that Naaman left behind in the Jordan lands on Gehazi. It's a heavy moment. I think this one hurts, so I'll let it stand as it is.
